catalog_locator: ch. 6 Tone, sec. 6.2 'Tone phonology', p. 104; sec. 7.4 'Tone', p. 116; lit. review sec. on tone, p. 39
catalog_quote: Current data provides evidence for two lexically contrastive tonemes, a high level tone, which is marked with an acute accent á, and a low level tone, which is marked with a grave accent à. The tone-bearing unit in Kufo appears to be the syllable. ... It is worth noting that tone contrasts have not yet been observed in monosyllabic words, which all appear to carry a high tone when elicited within a frame without a following long pause, and which carry a falling tone otherwise. Tonal minimal pairs are rare, and tone appears to have a low functional load both lexically and grammatically based on the data collected for the current project. ... [p.116] Kufo tone appears to be an inseparable component of the stems and is not altered during verb conjugations and noun singularisation or pluralisation. In future work, pitch conditioning and intonation will be particularly worth studying. ... In…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at pp.104 and 116 of the held Li 2022 PDF; 'stress' never occurs in the thesis. (2) The deciding source is a 2022 phonology thesis with acoustic tone data, the only phonology of this languoid; Glottolog's two descriptive refs are a morphology thesis and field notes. (3) I fetched sources all three reachable non-held descriptions (Hall & Hall 2004 OPSL 9 p.65; Mullan 2022 pp.15-16; Blench 2004 Ogmios): the first two independently state a two-tone (H/L, syllable TBU) system with lexical and grammatical function and say nothing about word stress; the third is silent. Nothing found suggests a stress/accent analysis exists for Kufo or any Kanga variety, so TONAL with domain UNSTATED stands. Minor standing caveat already in the record: kang1288 is Kanga as a whole while all sources describe the Kufo (Kufa-Lima) variety; Hall & Hall's Kanga/Kufa examples show the same two-to

sources.citation: Mullan, Keira. 2022. Nominal number and gender in Kufo: A description of its derivational and inflectional systems. BA Honours thesis, Australian National University. hdl:1885/282459 (254 pp PDF).
sources.quote: 'Kufo is a tonal language with both lexical and grammatical tone. Kufo has two tones, high and low, which are borne by the syllable. High tones are represented with an acute accent and low tones are unmarked.' with lexical (nyara 'cross cousin' / 'fences') and grammatical (present vs past of 'give') minimal pairs; defers phonology to Li (in prep.). grep 'stress' = 0 hits in the whole thesis.

sources.citation: Hall, Ed & Marian Hall. 2004. Kadugli-Krongo. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 57-68. SIL-Sudan. (via Wayback capture 20150513 of sil.org bitstream)
sources.quote: 'The tone system has not been fully analysed for any of the Kadugli-Krongo languages. ... The other Kadugli-Krongo languages that we have studied also have two tones, with a considerable amount of pitch conditioning. A few words in Kamda and in Kadugli seem to have a mid pitch also. In all of the languages there are only a limited number of lexical contrasts based on tone (example 23). Tone probably carries a greater grammatical functional load.' The only occurrence of 'stress' in the chapter is orthographic and hypothetical: '<x> was chosen so that there would be the possibility of adding dia
sources.locator: sec. 4.2 'Tone', p. 65 (example 23 is a Kufa tonal minimal pair nyaara 'female cousin' vs 'thorn fence (pl.)'); sec. 3.2.1 p. 62-63 only hypothetical mention of stress
